source.title: Modality-Aware Neuron Pruning for Unlearning in Multimodal Large Language Models
source.authors: Zhe-Yuan Liu; Guang-Yao Dou; Xiangchi Yuan; Chun-Hui Zhang; Zhao-Xuan Tan; Meng Jiang

page_placements.theme: Uneven transfer of unlearning across modalities and languages

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates unlearning in multimodal models and reports how results differ between multimodal and text-only inputs, a new setting for the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates unlearning performance and utility, but does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or adversarial prompt recovery. Its transformed Test Set combines paraphrased text with changed images, so it does not isolate prompt rephrasing. Figure 4 and Section 5.1 explicitly describe modality-dependent results; values not stated there are recorded qualitatively. The paper's other aggregate comparisons are not recovery-attack results.
record.test_reason: The study introduces MANU, a neuron-pruning unlearning method for multimodal LLMs (LLaVA-1.5-7B, Idefics2-8B, LLaVA-13B) on MLLMU-Bench. It reports forget-set accuracy against retain and utility accuracy, which bears on version A's 'near chance while keeping general ability' part in a new multimodal setting. It runs no recovery attacks: no relearning, ablation, quantization or jailbreaks. Robustness is left as future work. Its modality finding is that baselines unlearn image+text queries but not text-only ones. That is incomplete transfer of unlearning, not an attack restoring knowledge, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also argue that LLM unlearning methods applied to MLLMs leave knowledge in the text-only pathway (imbalanced unlearning), and that MANU fixes this. They call MANU preliminary: it has not reached an optimal unlearning–utility balance and its attack robustness is untested.
record.recipe_differences: MANU selects and prunes MLP neurons using modality-aware importance scores; the paper compares it with gradient-based unlearning, KL minimization, NPO, and prompting rather than reproducing the cited recovery attacks.
record.method_sensitivity: Pruning ratio changes both unlearning performance and retained utility. The reported unlearning results also differ between text-only and multimodal input for several baseline methods.

fits_no_version.finding: GA, Gradient Difference, KL and NPO unlearn strongly for image+text queries but leave target knowledge when the same facts are queried text-only (Fig. 4, 7–11; Fig. 2 heatmaps). MANU is described as balanced across modalities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multimodal LLMs, unlearning applied through multimodal inputs does not transfer to text-only queries, leaving the knowledge accessible.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The study's robustness against attacks is not tested, and the authors identify it as requiring further validation. The forgetting task uses fictitious profiles fine-tuned on the vanilla model. No uncertainty estimates are stated, and chance levels are not reported.
record.rows_left_out: No separate recovery-attack rows were available. The aggregate comparisons in Tables 1 and 4 and other utility results were not extracted as recovery evidence; the numeric pruning-ratio results in Table 2 and the explicit modality comparison in Section 5.1 were prioritized.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the forgotten knowledge. Chance level is not reported.
All: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
All: no direction ablation. The Fig. 2 heatmaps of residual knowledge by layer are descriptive and not a recovery test.
No jailbreaks or in-context attacks. The Test Set combines paraphrased text with transformed images, so rephrasing alone is not isolated.
MANU is not claimed to resist attacks; the authors say its robustness needs validation.

missing.what: Forget/Test/Retain/Real Celebrity accuracy for the baselines (GA, Grad. Diff., KL, NPO, Prompting) across 5/10/15% splits. Example: LLaVA 10%, GA forget 43.85% vs vanilla 49.15%, retain 41.91%.
General-ability benchmarks after unlearning, e.g. LLaVA MIA-Bench 69.60 vanilla vs 64.02 MANU and 57.29 GA.
MANU pruning-ratio results at the 5% and 15% splits
LLaVA-13B results at the 5% split (forget class. 44.40→33.65 for MANU)
Ablations of the importance functions (forget accuracy rises to 47.35% without I_freq)

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper on fictitious profiles fine-tuned into the model. Vanilla accuracy on forget MCQs is only about 49–54%, so the headroom to chance is small, and chance is never stated. No uncertainty estimates are given. No recovery attack is run, so the study cannot speak to the shallow-unlearning core (B–E).

versions.untested_parts: The paper measures unlearning performance and utility, but does not test whether simple attacks recover knowledge. It does not state chance levels.
Text and image transformations are combined in the Test Set; the effect of rephrasing prompts alone is not tested.

relationships.display_finding: Forget/test accuracy declined 10–19 points while retain accuracy changed approximately 2–8 points, leaving substantial target accuracy without an established chance baseline.
